One percentage point sounds small. Run it on a real loan.

$400,000 at 7.03% is about $2,669 a month.
The same loan at 6.03% is about $2,406.
That gap is $263 a month.

Over thirty years it is roughly $94,800 — a second deposit, paid to the bank instead.

My take: people shop the house for months and the rate for an afternoon.

A $5,000 card balance at 22%. The only difference is what you pay each month.

$150 a month clears it in 4 years 4 months, and costs $2,798 in interest.
$300 a month clears it in 1 year 9 months, and costs $1,022.

Same debt. Same rate. $1,776 difference.

My take: the card company sets the minimum. Everything above it is yours to decide.

Two letters apart. They sit on opposite sides of your money.

APR is what you are charged when you borrow.
APY is what you are paid when you save.
APY includes compounding. APR usually does not.

A bank will quote you whichever one looks better.

My take: read which letter is on the page before you read the number.

Do you know the APY on your own savings account?

Source: Truth in Savings Act definitions

$100,000 growing at 7% becomes about $761,000.

The late fee is the cheapest part.

A payment lands 30 days late.
It goes on your credit file and can sit there seven years.
A lower score raises the rate on the next loan you take.

The fee was $35. The score is what costs you.

My take: autopay the minimum on everything, then pay properly on top. The minimum is insurance, not a plan.

You have $1,000 spare. Two honest answers.

Paying down a 22% card is a guaranteed 22% return.
No savings account pays close to that.
But a card you have paid off is also a card you can run up again when the car breaks.

My take: a small cushion first, then attack the card. The cushion is what stops the card coming back.
